title: Superconducting Flux Memory for Cryogenic Applications
authors: Tony X. Zhou, John McFarland, Aruna N. Ramanayaka, Brian Sears, Colin Stack, Aref Fouladi, Robert Smith, Sambarta Rakshit, Zachary A. Stegen, Keith D. Hillaire, Moe Khalil, Robert M. Young, David G. Ferguson, Anthony J. Przybysz, John X. Pryzbysz, Mark Covington, Gregory R Boyd, Jeremy Clark, Aaron Pesetski
abstract: We report the development of flux memory for use with superconducting circuits. This technology stores persistent currents in superconducting loops on-chip to be used to provide flux biasing for superconducting circuits, like qubits. We developed three types of flux memory and draw comparisons among them for circuit design. We demonstrate the utility of flux memory by using an in-situ flux detector and characterize each approach and further demonstrate that once flux is set in a memory cell, benchtop DC control sources can be powered off, leaving the on-chip flux bias in place. We propose that flux memory can be arranged in a two-dimensional configuration to multiplex control signals and reduce how line counts scale (N^2 devices -> 2N control lines), and our experimental results pave the path to the proposed scalability. We demonstrate the use of flux memory to flux bias a transmon qubit and show the tunability of the qubit state to a target frequency which remained stable on-chip for 20 hours.
summary: This paper reports on the design and experimental validation of superconducting flux memory devices intended to provide persistent, on-chip flux biasing for superconducting qubits. By developing three distinct memory types, the authors demonstrate a scalable method to reduce external control wiring complexity. The successful demonstration of stable flux biasing for over 20 hours paves the way for larger, more integrated quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for on-chip, persistent flux biasing sources for superconducting quantum circuits, such as qubits, to reduce the complexity of external control wiring.
main_result: The authors successfully developed and demonstrated three types of flux memory (SJJ, Flux Lock, Htron) that can store a stable DC flux bias for extended periods (over 20 hours), enabling scalable qubit control.
method: The research involves developing superconducting circuits, simulating their behavior using SPICE, and experimentally characterizing the programmable flux storage and output using in-situ flux detectors.
model_or_system: The core system is superconducting flux memory, implemented in three forms: Single Josephson Junction (SJJ), Flux Lock (requiring two JJs), and a Josephson Junction-free Cryotron (htron). These are designed to store persistent currents in superconducting loops.
key_observables: Stored flux (measured in units of flux quanta, $\Phi_0$), qubit state tunability frequency, and the achievable step size of the flux bias.
important_parameters: The ability to scale control lines from $N^2$ to $2N$ in a 2D array is a key parameter demonstrating scalability. The stability time of 20 hours is a critical performance metric.
main_assumptions: The primary limitations noted are the potential energy barrier depth limiting storage, and that the current simulation does not include kinetic inductance effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematics of the three memory types, the proposed 2D addressing scheme, and experimental results showing the flux biasing of a transmon qubit with stable frequency shifts over time.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of control line scaling, details the three memory architectures (SJJ, Flux Lock, Htron), presents the methods for programming and characterizing each type, and culminates in experimental demonstrations of using the memory to bias and tune a transmon qubit.
why_interesting: The development of robust, on-chip, and persistent control elements like flux memory is crucial for scaling up quantum processors, directly impacting the feasibility of large-scale quantum computation architectures.

Fig. 4. Schematic of the tunable resonator flux detector. There is an independent bias line to verify that the tunable resonator yielded and functions above the SQUID, otherwise the SQUID bias comes from the flux memory through a mutual inductor. The SQUID can be thought of as a tunable inductance, thus shifting the resonant frequency of the LC-circuit comprised of a SQUID and resonator when flux is applied to its loop.
